On the last Sunday of every month, my father sharpened the kitchen knives and then, because the stone was already wet, asked around the building if anyone had a pair of scissors that needed doing.

He always asked as though he’d only just thought of it. By the time I was ten, Mrs. Ortiz downstairs was laying hers out the night before.

I got the job of returning them. This was better than sharpening. You got to see little slices of other people’s Sundays: a man in good trousers ironing his shirt with no shirt on; two girls giving a doll a bath in a salad spinner; Mrs. Ortiz at the table with a newspaper, drinking coffee out of a cup so thin I could see the dark line of it through the china.

She tested her scissors on the margin of the paper. One clean snip. “Tell him they’re terrible,” she said, and put two warm rolls in a bag for me to take upstairs.

When my father moved into a smaller place, I found the stone behind the bread box. I have it now. It’s gray, with a shallow dip in the middle, and I’m not especially good with it. Last month I did my own scissors and then stood in the hall for a while, feeling foolish. Across the landing, somebody had taped a drawing of a purple horse to their door.

I knocked anyway.

The man who answered thought for a moment. “Kitchen ones or sewing ones?”

I hadn’t known there would be a question. “Let’s start with the kitchen ones,” I said.
